They know about the house. Every piece of furniture, the rugs, the clothes in my closet... it's all steeped in this toxic rot. And the neighbors, they can sense it. They look at me like I'm the one who brought this sickness into the neighborhood. Like I'm a failure for not being able to stop it. So they just wait. They want to see the exact moment I completely break under the weight of it all. They aren't worried about my health. They just want to be there when I finally, completely fail. Because they know I can't fix the wiring. They know the mold has already won. So no, it's not concern at all. It's just... it's just this constant, heavy judgment while I'm trapped inside a house that is literally destroying me and everything I have.

It's so incredibly exhausting to live like this every single minute of the day, never knowing why I can see the water but can't feel it.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself having trouble putting your thoughts into words when trying to explain what's happening with the house?\n\nPatient: Putting my thoughts into words... yeah. Yeah, it's... it's like trying to wade through wet cement. That's the only way I can describe it. Actually, my wife, she was just saying the other day that I move like I'm underwater now. And she's right, she really is. It’s not just that I can’t find the right words, it’s that the whole process of thinking and speaking and just existing feels so impossibly slow and heavy. \n\nLike, just the other day, we were trying to figure out what to do, and someone was asking me a very simple question about a repair estimate. I think it was about replacing some of the baseboards, or maybe the drywall where the water was—I don't even remember the exact details because it all just blurs together into this big, overwhelming mess of ruin. But they asked me this basic, straightforward question, something I should have been able to answer in two seconds. And I just... I stood there. I could hear the question echoing in my head, I knew I needed to answer, but getting my mouth to open and actually form the words... it took so long. \n\nIt took so incredibly long that they just gave up. They just started talking for me. People do that a lot now. They ask me something, wait a few seconds, and then just fill in the blank themselves because I’m just standing there, staring, trying to push through this heavy, suffocating water just to get a single sentence out. It makes me feel completely useless. I mean, how can I explain what's really happening with the house, how can I make anyone understand the poison and the rot, when I can't even answer a basic question about an estimate without someone else having to step in and speak for me? It's just... it's like my brain and my body have completely ground to a halt under the weight of it all. Everything is just so slow now.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt an overwhelming sense of fear or anxiety when you think about the poison in your house?\n\nPatient: Fear? No... no, I wouldn't use that word. Anxiety... that's not it either. I mean, anxiety is what you feel when you're waiting for the other shoe to drop, right? It’s for the 'what ifs.' Like, what if the car breaks down, or what if you lose your job. My wife, she gets anxious. She paces around the kitchen, wringing her hands, trying to figure out how to fix things that are already completely broken. But me? When I think about the poison... the mold, the contamination in everything we own... I don't feel fear. \n\nIt’s more like... it’s just this absolute, crushing certainty. Why would I be afraid of something that has already won? You don't feel anxious when you're already drowning at the bottom of the ocean, you just feel the pressure of the water pressing down on you from all sides. That's what it is for me. Just this immense pressure.
